name: Void
label: Dischord
lede: Four Columbia, Maryland teenagers started a band in 1980, played each part as fast as they could, and ended up on one side of a split LP with Faith that people are still arguing about. The album they made after it never came out.

eras.title: Nothing to do in a model town
eras.text: Columbia, Maryland was one of the first planned communities in the country: tidy lawns, organized everything, thirty miles north of Washington. Dischord's own history calls it the perfect birthplace for a band as chaotic as Void.

q: Your lawn had to look a certain way.
years.src: Washington City Paper: Void discusses · Wikipedia: Void (band)
years.h: Four Columbia High kids name their band after a Black Sabbath song
years.p: [[John Weiffenbach|c415a399-2299-4899-b0d7-5fb1087e0c0f]], [[Bubba Dupree|faa35f26-bda4-4dd0-9d92-121e616d955a]], [[Chris Stover|e8c9149b-3ac0-4852-8425-3b9d6e8c0b53]] and [[Sean Finnegan|b5dac872-bd13-49df-b97f-f81c16f003ed]] start Void, taking the name from Black Sabbath's Into the Void.
years.xp:
Columbia offered sports and hanging around, and not much else. Dupree told Washington City Paper it was "mostly populated by rednecks and idealistic ex-hippies" with "absolutely nothing to do," so any excuse to get to a show in D.C. or Baltimore was a good one.

Stover's way in ran through Oddfellows Hall in Towson, where he saw [[The Teen Idles|84e8d8bf-da21-4488-89e5-50a4c12ff4fa]] and met [[Ian MacKaye|c12f644b-1066-4ead-b0dd-d0c380f5cca2]] and [[Jeff Nelson|51f7994c-949d-4dbe-89eb-2c33f42a5620]]. He remembers the D.C. crowd's reaction as "Holy shit, what the hell is going on?"

years.h: Void make their D.C. debut at a fifteen-band Wilson Center marathon
years.p: Bad Brains largely organized the bill. Dischord says Void played as if each member was going as fast as he could, not necessarily together.
years.xp: Dischord's account is that some in the room heard complete cacophony and others heard music on a higher level. Wikipedia places the first D.C. show in early 1981 instead; this page follows Dischord.

eras.title: Thirty songs, two sessions
eras.text: Void cut thirty songs across two 1981 sessions, a month apart. The Hit and Run tapes sat unheard for three decades. The Inner Ear tapes put them on Dischord's first compilation, Flex Your Head.

years.src: Washington City Paper: Faith and Void
years.h: Void go to Arlington and cut ten songs in December
years.p: Inner Ear gives up the Flex Your Head tracks and, a decade later, the Condensed Flesh seven-inch. It comes a month after Void's twenty-song Hit and Run session.
years.xp: Washington City Paper heard "a newly nihilistic Void" on the Inner Ear tapes, with Dupree's heavy-rock guitar pushed further forward.

eras.title: Half an LP with Faith
eras.text: 1982 was Void's year on record. They made the Dischord sampler, played New York, and split an LP with Faith: two bands, two ideas of speed, one sleeve.

years.h: Three Void songs land on Flex Your Head
years.p: Dehumanized, Authority and My Rules sit on Dischord's compilation next to [[Minor Threat|09037f07-42bc-46ac-a1ee-37f834451fee]], [[The Teen Idles|84e8d8bf-da21-4488-89e5-50a4c12ff4fa]] and [[SOA|e54cb250-3502-4c32-9482-70488bd9a8cb]].

years.h: A band with nothing to do in Columbia plays CBGB
years.p: Void start touring the Northeast in mid-1982, with a stop at CBGB in New York.

years.src: Washington City Paper: Faith and Void · Dischord: Faith/Void · Wikipedia: Void (band)
yt: Live at the Wilson Center, D.C., Oct. 22, 1982
years.p: Twelve Void songs recorded with Don Zientara at Inner Ear in June 1982 take one side; [[Faith|f735a867-9a16-451f-8f83-669ed42e2574]] take the other. Critic Doug Mosurock later called Void's side quintessential American hardcore.
years.xp:
Fans used to ask, "Are you a Faith person or a Void person?" Washington City Paper reports that more out-of-towners picked Void.

[[Ian MacKaye|c12f644b-1066-4ead-b0dd-d0c380f5cca2]] pitched pairing the two bands, and Void were happy to join the Dischord family. Faith are tight and furious; Void sound like four people falling down a staircase in formation.

The record outlived both bands. Dischord reissued it in 1985 and again in a remastered edition in 2008.

eras.title: The album nobody put out
eras.text: Void signed with Touch and Go and made a full album. The band ended first, the record stayed on the shelf, and bootleggers eventually found it as Potions for Bad Dreams.

years.src: Wikipedia: Void (band) · Washington City Paper: Void discusses · Washington City Paper: Faith and Void
years.h: Touch and Go gets a finished Void album, then no Void
years.p: Void sign with Touch and Go and record a full album. By the time it could come out the band is gone, and label owner Corey Rusk isn't interested in releasing an album by a band that no longer exists.
years.xp:
The tapes got around anyway, and bootleggers circulated the session as Potions for Bad Dreams. According to Wikipedia, citing Stover's Vice interview, [[White Zombie|cfe572bf-840f-4bed-934a-f69f4b1e90d4]] and [[Melvins|9ccfbc94-a4f4-42f7-b6f5-d903ab77cccb]] have said it shaped their own sound.

Stover's take, to Washington City Paper: "Some things are better left unreleased." Dupree refused to see it out.

years.src: Dischord: Void · Washington City Paper: Void discusses
years.h: Void end in the fall of 1984
years.p: Dischord dates the breakup to fall 1984. Of the four, only Bubba Dupree keeps making music.
years.xp: Dupree told Washington City Paper he graduated in 1983, the year Wikipedia and the paper give for the end. Dischord's dates run later, and this page uses them.

eras.title: The reputation grows without them
eras.text: With Void gone, the records did the work. Dischord reissued Faith/Void, and the small label Eye 95 gave the Inner Ear session its own seven-inch, Condensed Flesh.

years.p: The 1982 split LP gets its first reissue, three years after it came out.

years.h: Eye 95 gives the Inner Ear tapes a seven-inch
years.p: Condensed Flesh collects songs from Void's December 1981 session, including Black, Jewish & Poor and War Hero.

eras.title: Emptying the vaults
eras.text: Void's afterlife picked up speed in the 2000s: drummer Sean Finnegan died, Faith/Void was remastered, and Dischord's archive release Sessions 1981-83 put out twenty songs few outside the band had heard.

years.p: Void's drummer, who played on every record the band made, dies of an apparent heart attack, Dischord reported. He had been working on the set of HBO's The Wire.
years.xp: His family held the viewing in Ellicott City, Maryland, not far from Columbia, and asked for donations to the Fisher House at Walter Reed in place of flowers.

years.p: Dischord releases a digitally remastered edition of the 1982 split LP.

years.src: Dischord: Void, Sessions · Washington City Paper: Void discusses
years.h: Void's Hit and Run tapes come out after 30 years in a box
years.p: The twenty-song November 1981 session appears in 2011 as Sessions 1981-83, with the Inner Ear tapes, Faith/Void outtakes and two songs from a July 1983 show.
years.xp:
Steve Carr recorded the Hit and Run session. Dupree told Washington City Paper, "I don't even remember recording most of it." Stover: "I think the real surprise was how much shit Ian had in his archives."

MacKaye mixed the set, which was pressed on blue vinyl as Dischord No. 171.

years.h: Bubba Dupree joins 3rd Secret in Seattle
years.p: The Void guitarist, who spent the 1990s and 2000s guesting with Soundgarden, Moby and [[Dave Grohl|4d5f891d-9bce-45ae-ad86-912dd27252fa]], joins a band built around former members of Nirvana and Soundgarden.
Eye 95 marks 30 years of the 1992 seven-inch with an edition on translucent gold-orange vinyl.
